title: Eugene Wright facing prejudice in the quartet and on southern tours
summary: Gene Wright dealt with criticism from black musicians and segregation; Dave canceled concerts in the South when Gene was not accepted.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: And Joe and Gene — and then right, like my parents always had great admiration for Gene in terms of his personality. Like he was just a guy — Gene was very special not only from his musical point of view but people have to realize that Gene had to deal with being in the quartet and being wildly successful and a little bit parallel to like Jackie Robinson. Other black musicians were giving him crap about, “You’re playing with these white guys? Why are you playing with these white guys.” You know, “the white guys are
stealing our music” and all that kind of crap. And Gene just handled it with typical diplomacy and grace. I don’t know maybe that’s how he got the name “Senator.”

You know and then also he had to deal with prejudice everywhere, like the tours of the south where they would say, “You can’t go on stage with that guy,” and you know all that kind of stuff. Dave canceled huge amounts of concerts in the south, I forget how many there were, like 23 concerts or something where when they found out that — because the quartet before they got Gene it was an all-white group.
I think Norman Bates was the bass player.

You know and on Jazz Goes to College and all that. So the image is oh great, it’s a white jazz group, that’ll fly. So once there was the addition of Gene then you know they weren’t so sure they wanted that on stage.
